title: India Is Preparing to Let Its Fiscal Deficit Blow Past Target. The Iran War Left No Choice.
excerpt: Authorities are willing to widen the gap to 4.8 per cent of GDP — half a percentage point above February's goal — as energy subsidies devour the budget.
body:
India's government is quietly preparing to abandon one of its most closely guarded fiscal targets. Authorities are willing to let the budget deficit widen by as much as half a percentage point to 4.8 per cent of GDP, up from the 4.3 per cent goal Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman set in February, according to a Bloomberg News report citing an official familiar with the matter.

The culprit is the Iran war, and more specifically, the cost of shielding 1.4 billion people from its consequences.

## The Subsidy Squeeze

India imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil. When the Strait of Hormuz was effectively shut in March, Brent crude spiked above $100 a barrel and has hovered between $85 and $95 since. Every dollar increase in oil prices costs the Indian exchequer approximately $2 billion a year in additional subsidies on cooking gas, kerosene, and fertiliser — the last of which has already doubled in cost since March.

The government's fertiliser subsidy bill alone is on track to overshoot its full-year allocation of ₹1.64 lakh crore before the kharif planting season is over. Cooking gas subsidies, which New Delhi had been systematically rolling back for years, are now being expanded again as LPG cylinder prices crossed ₹1,100 in several states.

"The February budget was written in a world where Brent was at $75 and the Strait of Hormuz was open," said a former member of the Fifteenth Finance Commission who declined to be named. "Neither assumption holds."

## What Changed Between February and Now

When Sitharaman presented the Union Budget on February 1, the fiscal consolidation glide path was the government's proudest macroeconomic achievement. The deficit had been brought down from 6.4 per cent in 2022-23 to 4.8 per cent in 2024-25, and the 4.3 per cent target for 2026-27 was supposed to put India on track to breach the 3 per cent threshold by 2028-29.

Then the United States and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran on February 28. Three months later, the war has killed thousands, the Strait remains contested, and India's fuel import bill has ballooned by an estimated ₹1.2 lakh crore over initial projections.

Revenue, meanwhile, has not kept pace. GST collections have held steady but personal income tax growth has slowed as the services sector, rattled by global uncertainty and an AI-driven pullback in IT hiring, underperforms expectations.

## Markets Are Already Moving

The news broke overnight while Indian markets were closed, but early signals on Friday suggest a mixed reception. Bond traders had largely priced in some fiscal slippage — the 10-year benchmark yield has been creeping upward since May — but a full half-percentage-point deviation from target is at the outer edge of expectations.

Short-term government bond yields fell sharply this week after the RBI announced subsidised forex swaps for NRI deposits, creating a rare divergence between the short and long ends of the curve. If the wider deficit pushes long-end yields higher still, that spread could widen to levels not seen since the pandemic.

The rupee, already under pressure from oil company dollar demand, had settled at 95.76 per dollar on Thursday. A wider fiscal deficit adds another structural headwind, though Friday's Iran deal optimism — Brent fell to a two-month low of $88.80 — could offset the immediate impact.

## What This Means for NRIs

For the millions of Non-Resident Indians who maintain rupee-denominated investments, the fiscal slippage is a signal to watch closely.

A wider deficit typically means more government borrowing, which can crowd out private investment and push up interest rates. For NRIs holding Indian government bonds through recently expanded foreign investor limits, higher yields could mean mark-to-market losses in the short term but better reinvestment opportunities ahead.

The RBI's aggressive push to attract NRI deposits — with banks now offering up to 7.1 per cent on FCNR deposits after a 300-basis-point hike this week — takes on added significance. New Delhi needs every dollar it can attract to fund the growing deficit without destabilising the currency.

"The deficit number matters less than the quality of spending," said Ashwin Patni, head of wealth management solutions at Julius Baer India. "If the additional spending goes to fuel subsidies rather than infrastructure, the growth multiplier is much lower."

## The Bigger Picture

India is not alone in facing war-driven fiscal pressure. Across oil-importing Asia, governments from Thailand to the Philippines are wrestling with the same calculus of subsidies versus inflation versus voter anger.

But India's situation carries particular weight because of its size and its aspirations. The country is in the middle of a generational infrastructure build-out — highways, ports, railways, semiconductor fabs — and every rupee diverted to fuel subsidies is a rupee not spent on productive capital.

Reuters reported it has sought comment from India's finance ministry. Until an official response comes, the 4.8 per cent figure remains what it is: a signal that even the most disciplined fiscal managers in emerging markets cannot outrun a war that has redrawn the global energy map.

**Sources**: Bloomberg News, Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, Reserve Bank of India
